newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: PRESS DIGEST - South Africa - March 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - South Africa - March 13.

text.p: These are the leading stories in the South African press on Thursday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
BUSINESS DAY
- Finance Minister Trevor Manuel delivered on his promise to place South Africa on a road of fiscal rectitude, containing overall spending to a mere 6.1 percent increase in the 1997/98 fiscal year.
- Manuel announced moves to ease exchange controls which included allowing individuals to invest in foreign currency for the first time in decades.

- The government would go to the local capital market for 27.7 billion rand, down from last year's 34.2 billion rand, for the bulk of its budgeted gross borrowing requirement in the 1997/98 fiscal year, Manuel disclosed.

- Tough action would be taken against tax evaders and non-payers who would be excluded from tendering for lucrative contracts, would be unable to benefit from government incentive schemes and would be denied foreign currency, Manuel announced.

- Six former Natal security branch policemen have led "truth commission" investigators to the graves of 10 activists they murdered during the 1980s, confirming the existence of another regional death squad.
BUSINESS REPORT
- Industrial share prices took a slight knock on Wednesday following the release of the budget, but the rand took strength on positive announcements about exchange controls, dealers said.
- The Reserve Bank has repeated its call to the government to increase the pace of implementation of fiscal discipline and economic reform in its March quarterly bulletin released on Wednesday.

- Share price moves before and after cautionary notices issued this year for several Johannesburg Stock Exchange-listed companies suggest some insider trading, says Peter Urbani, a portfolio manager at Commercial Union Investment management.

- Khula Enterprise, the body set up by the Trade and Industry Department to provide finance for small, medium and micro businesses, would be concluding an agreement with the Post Office for the granting of loans to small businesses, Khula chief executive Sizwe Tati said.
SAKE-BEELD
- South African financial markets reacted very positively to the budget.
- The relaxation of exchange controls announced in the budget should have just a small effect on the rand when the measures come into effect on July 1.
- One positive result of the weakening of the rand over the past year has been a solid increase in the value of goods exported since the fourth quarter.
- A small proportion of the housing budget, 819 million rand, is expected to be left over from the last financial year, compared with the 2.5 billion rand of a year earlier.
BEELD

- Finance Minister Manuel's budget takes from the rich to give to the poor. Not much could be found to be wrong with that, but some people in the higher tax brackets might think the goose with the golden eggs has been slaughtered.
- Organisers of Wednesday's disastrous Zulu gathering in Johannesburg could face prosecution. Three people were killed and a dozen hurt in the demonstration.
THE STAR
- Finance Minister Manuel's debut "people's budget" has been praised by most political parties and welcomed by big business.
- Three people were killed when the Johannesburg city centre erupted into chaos on Wednesday as groups of marchers, commemorating shootings in 1994, shot indiscriminately into the air.

- A multibillion-rand pipeline carrying millions of tonnes of magnetite through the middle of the Kruger National Park is being planned by the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC), Palabora Mining Co Ltd and Foskor.
SOWETAN
- Finance Minister Manuel's first budget focused on social, protection and economic services but offered little respite to those in the high income bracket.
